text: If you've used conventional antiperspirant for years, your body has adapted to it. Antiperspirants work by physically plugging your sweat ducts with aluminum compounds, stopping something your body is built to do. Stop using them, and your body needs time to adjust. That window is usually somewhere between one and four weeks, and it varies person to person. During that stretch, you might notice: More sweating than usual, as the ducts that were plugged open back up Odour that's stronger or different than what you're used to, as your skin's bacteria rebalance Some underarm sensitivity None of that means the deodorant isn't working. It means your body's doing exactly what it's supposed to do once you take the plug out. MAKING THE SWITCH EASIER 1. Time it right. Start during a lower-pressure stretch if you can such as a slower week, a break from the gym, whatever gives your body room to adjust without a big presentation riding on it. 2. Stay consistent. Apply every morning, even on days you don't think you need it. Consistency is what gets your underarm bacteria to settle faster. 3. Keep things clean. Wash daily with a gentle, pH-balanced cleanser. It clears out odour-causing bacteria without stripping your skin, which makes the whole adjustment period shorter and easier. 4. Reapply if you need to. In the first couple of weeks, a midday touch-up on a high-activity day is normal. It doesn't mean the formula's failing you. 5. Start with the right formula. If your skin runs sensitive, a baking soda-free formula from day one makes the whole thing easier. Irritated skin and a thrown-off pH just slow everything down. WHAT TO EXPECT Most people are through the adjustment within one to four weeks with some faster, some slower. Sweat and odour tend to be most noticeable early on and settle as your body catches up. If you're still uncomfortable well past the month mark, that's worth a closer look at the formula, not something to push through. A NOTE ON SWEATING Natural deodorant doesn't stop you from sweating, and that's the point. Sweating is how your body regulates temperature. It's not something to block, it's something to work with. A good natural deodorant neutralizes odour. It doesn't shut down a system your body needs. BPM uses magnesium hydroxide and tapioca starch to absorb moisture and neutralize odour, without interfering with what your body's actually trying to do. Browse the full Natural Deodorant collection to find your fit. YOU WON'T WANT TO GO BACK The adjustment period can feel discouraging in the moment. Most people who push through it land somewhere better with less irritation, and the simple upside of knowing exactly what's in the tube.

Baking soda has a pH of around 8–9. Your skin sits around 4.5–5.5. That's not a small gap. It's the difference between your skin's protective acid mantle staying intact and getting knocked off balance. For a lot of people, that imbalance shows up fast: Redness and irritation Burning or stinging Rashes and contact dermatitis Over time, in some cases, patches of darker skin where the irritation kept coming back Not everyone reacts. Some people wear baking soda deodorant for years without issue. But "some people are fine" isn't the same as "it's fine" and if your skin has ever gone from calm to angry a few days into a new natural deodorant, baking soda is the usual suspect. WHY IT'S STILL EVERYWHERE Baking soda works. It neutralizes the bacteria that cause odour, it's cheap, and it's easy to source, which is exactly why it became the default in early natural deodorants. None of that makes it a good match for every underarm. It just makes it a convenient one. WHAT WE USE INSTEAD Ditching baking soda doesn't mean giving up odour protection. It means picking ingredients that do the same job without the same fallout: Magnesium hydroxide — neutralizes odour-causing bacteria the same way baking soda does, but through a slow, steady release instead of a sharp pH spike. It's not a "gentler pH" as magnesium hydroxide is actually more alkaline than baking soda on paper. The difference is timing: it dissolves gradually in sweat instead of hitting your skin all at once, which is why skin that reacts to baking soda often tolerates it fine. Tapioca starch — absorbs moisture and keeps the formula gliding on instead of sitting gritty. Plant-based oils and emulsifiers — condition the skin instead of stripping it. This is the formula we build BPM around. No baking soda. No aluminum. Zinc and magnesium doing the actual work, nothing extra along for the ride. Check out our Sensitive Skin Deodorant collection or browse the full Natural Deodorant range. HOW TO TELL IF BAKING SODA IS THE PROBLEM If a natural deodorant has left you red, itchy, or burning, baking soda is the most common cause. Reaction timelines vary. For some people it's days, for others it takes longer to build up so don't rule it out just because the first week was fine. The upside: switching to a baking soda-free formula is usually enough to let skin recover. How long that takes depends on the person and how irritated things got, so we won't put a number on it we can't back up. BOTTOM LINE Baking soda isn't dangerous. It's just not built for every underarm, and a lot of "natural deodorant doesn't work for me" stories are really "baking soda doesn't work for me" stories. If yours is one of them, the fix isn't giving up on natural deodorant, it's finding a formula that skips the ingredient causing the problem.
